claims.statement: The pectoralis major has two heads: a clavicular head from the inner half of the collarbone and a sternocostal head from the breastbone, the upper six rib cartilages and the tendon sheet of the outer abdominal muscle. Both attach to the upper-arm bone near the shoulder. Acting together they draw the arm in toward the body (adduction), turn it inward (internal rotation) and bring it across the chest. Acting apart, the clavicular head raises the arm forward (flexion) and the sternocostal head brings a raised arm back down (extension).

claims.statement: Bench-press studies measured upper-chest activity at different bench angles and do not fully agree. In 15 men pressing at four angles, the clavicular head was more active at inclines of 44 and 56 degrees than on a flat bench. In 30 trained adults, the upper portion of the muscle was most active at a 30-degree incline, and above 45 degrees front-deltoid activity rose while the pectoralis major's performance fell. In an older study of 6 men, the clavicular head was no more active on an incline than on a flat bench, and less active on a decline. These are short-term activity measurements; they do not show which angle grows the muscle more.

Parent node, neither drawn nor selectable (§1.2, §7.3): its actions are declared on the two heads, as the upper arm does for the triceps group. A generic test like the forearm's 'every muscle has a prime action' must skip parents (the pectoralis major is kind 'muscle').

UW and TeachMeAnatomy say the pectoralis major draws the scapula forward and down; it attaches to the upper-arm bone, not the shoulder blade, so the effect is through the arm. Listing it would offer the pectoralis major as a shoulder-blade target.
StatPearls says protraction 'allows for anteversion of the arm'; that is a shoulder-blade action that helps the arm forward, not a shoulder-joint action of the serratus.
Both can help lift ribs in forced breathing; there is no action id and it moves no load. Said in the pectoralis minor's claim.

actions.label: Horizontal adduction
actions.plainDescription: With the arm raised to shoulder height, brings it forward and across the front of the chest.
actions.note: Shared with the shoulders (§1.2); proposed wording for the shared library.

actions.label: Shoulder flexion
actions.plainDescription: Raises the arm forward and up in front of the body.
actions.note: Word for word as the upper-arm dossier proposed; one definition in the shared library.

actions.label: Shoulder extension
actions.plainDescription: Brings the arm down and back from in front of the body, and on behind it.
actions.note: Word for word as the upper-arm dossier proposed. The sternocostal head does only the first half (down from in front); its node action says so.

actions.label: Shoulder adduction
actions.plainDescription: Brings the arm down and in toward the side of the body.
actions.note: Shared with the back (§1.2); proposed wording.

actions.label: Internal rotation
actions.plainDescription: Turns the upper arm inward, so the forearm swings in toward the body (with the elbow bent).
actions.note: Shared with the shoulders (§1.2); proposed wording, following the forearm's 'with the elbow bent' convention for rotations.

actions.label: Shoulder-blade protraction
actions.plainDescription: Moves the shoulder blade forward around the rib cage, away from the spine, as when pushing the arms forward.

actions.label: Shoulder-blade depression
actions.plainDescription: Draws the shoulder blade down, away from the ear and toward the hip.
actions.note: Shared with the back (§1.2); proposed wording.

actions.label: Upward rotation
actions.plainDescription: Turns the shoulder blade so the shoulder socket faces upward, which lets the arm be raised above shoulder height.
actions.note: Shared with the shoulders and back (§1.2); proposed wording. The socket-faces-up wording is the usual definition; no claim cites it.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Thorax, Serratus Anterior Muscles

sources.title: Kenhub: pectoralis major muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q2, Q11, Q38): as a whole the muscle adducts and internally rotates the arm at the shoulder; acting independently the clavicular part helps flex the extended arm up to 90 degrees, while the sternocostal part extends the flexed arm by pulling it downwards; in males it is covered by deep fascia, subcutaneous tissue and skin; the tendons of the two heads twist into an anterior (clavicular) and a posterior (sternocostal) lamina. A Kenhub video transcript says the muscle rotates the arm outwards, which conflicts with the written pages; the video is not cited.

sources.title: Kenhub: upper limb muscles and movements
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q2): the clavicular head makes the pectoralis major a flexor of the arm at the shoulder and the sternocostal head an extensor; acting as a unit the muscle is a medial rotator and adductor of the arm.

sources.title: Kenhub: glenohumeral (shoulder) joint
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q56): the prime flexors of the glenohumeral joint are the deltoid (anterior fibres) and the pectoralis major (clavicular fibres); adduction is produced by the pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi and teres major, called the 'climbing muscles' as powerful adductors.

sources.title: Kenhub: pectoralis minor muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q24, Q31, Q41): lies deep only to the pectoralis major, which is its main front relation and almost completely covers it; from the third to fifth ribs to the coracoid process; protracts the scapula with the serratus anterior, can forcefully depress it, rotates it downward (medially), and with the scapula fixed helps raise ribs three to five in forced breathing. The summaries did not always say which Kenhub page (this one, the scapula page or the shoulder-girdle page) each action came from; innervation was given inconsistently and is not used.

sources.title: Kenhub: serratus anterior muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q31, Q35, Q37, Q40): a fan-shaped muscle on the side wall of the thorax whose main part lies deep under the scapula and the pectoral muscles; three parts, superior (ribs 1 to 2 to the superior angle), intermediate and inferior (ribs 4 to 8 or 9 to the medial border and inferior angle), the inferior part the most prominent and powerful; the whole muscle moves the scapula forward and sideways along the ribs and stabilises it; the inferior part's pull lets the arm be raised above 90 degrees; easy to palpate between the pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi, and in athletic bodies may be visible along the ribs underneath the axilla. One summary (Q31) said the superior part pulls the scapula downward; the German Kenhub page (Q35) says the superior part elevates the scapula and lowers the glenoid. Neither is used for an action.

sources.title: TeachMeAnatomy: muscles of the pectoral region
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q8, Q27, Q38; with the site's encyclopaedia pages on the pectoralis major and minor, which gave the same facts): the pectoralis major is the most superficial muscle of the pectoral region, fan-shaped, with a clavicular head from the front of the medial clavicle and a sternocostal head from the sternum, the upper six costal cartilages and the external oblique aponeurosis, both attaching at the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus; it adducts and medially rotates the arm and draws the scapula forward and down, and the clavicular head acting alone flexes the arm. sources.title: Radiopaedia: pectoralis major muscle

sources.title: Lulic-Kuryllo, Negro, Jiang and Dickerson, Differential regional pectoralis major activation indicates functional diversity in healthy females (Journal of Biomechanics 133:110966, 2022)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q13, Q15, Q21; abstract, the UWSpace accepted manuscript record and the PubMed record): high-density surface EMG of the clavicular, superior sternocostal and middle sternocostal regions in 29 healthy young women, two experiments, ramp-and-hold isometric tasks at several force levels. The middle sternocostal region was 12 to 108 per cent more active than the other two regions in extension, adduction with external rotation and high-elevation internal rotation; in forward and horizontal flexion the three regions were similar at every force level except forward flexion at 25 per cent of maximal force, where the clavicular region was 21 per cent more active than the superior sternocostal region; in low-elevation internal rotation the clavicular and middle sternocostal regions were more active than the superior sternocostal region. Acute isometric activity in women only, not growth.

singleSourceFunctionClaims: None. Each of the five function claims rests on six or more references: chest.pec_major (7), chest.pec_major_clavicular (9), chest.pec_major_sternocostal (8), chest.pec_minor (6), chest.serratus_anterior (9).

Each study's abstract was seen in two or three independent search summaries that agreed.
theHeadSplit: Supported by the function claims. Head-specific actions are named by StatPearls (NBK525991), Kenhub (two pages), IMAIOS, the UW atlas, TeachMeAnatomy and the PMC case report: the clavicular head flexes the arm, the sternocostal head extends a flexed arm; together they adduct and turn the arm inward. Loyola and Elsevier name no extension, and Elsevier calls the clavicular head's flexion 'assisting': the claims say so.

Muscle-activity evidence supports half of the split clearly. In isometric tasks (pmid.35093733) the middle sternocostal region was much more active than the clavicular region in extension and in adduction with the arm turned out, but in forward and horizontal flexion the three regions were about equally active, except forward pushing at a quarter of maximal force, where the clavicular region was more active than the upper sternocostal region. Bench-press studies disagree on whether an incline raises clavicular activity (lww.chest_press_angles yes at 44 and 56 degrees; pmid.33049982 most at 30 degrees; bisp.bench_press_five_shoulder_muscles no). The split therefore stands on anatomy, and the claims say that the forward-raising difference is not a measured difference in activity.

disagreementsAndWording: Clavicular head in raising the arm: main (IMAIOS 'primary action'; Kenhub 'prime flexors' with the anterior deltoid; StatPearls; UW; TeachMeAnatomy) against 'assists' (Elsevier) and 'secondary' for the whole muscle (Radiopaedia). The claim says one quick reference calls it assisting; the node action is prime.

Sternocostal head bringing the arm down: named by StatPearls, Kenhub, UW, IMAIOS ('contributes') and the PMC case report; not listed by Loyola or Elsevier. The claim says two references do not list it. The node action is prime, flagged for review ('assist' is defensible from IMAIOS's word).

Misattributed wording caught: one summary (Q11) attributed 'the muscle fibers attaching to the sternocostal head permit the horizontal and vertical adduction, extension, and internal rotation' to StatPearls; an exact-phrase search (Q62) found it is Wikipedia's wording. StatPearls is not cited for horizontal adduction; Radiopaedia ('bring the humerus across the chest') and Elsevier ('transversely adducts') carry it, with regional EMG beside them.
Kenhub video transcript says the pectoralis major turns the arm outward; Kenhub's written pages and every other reference say inward. The video is not cited.

Decline bench: Barnett et al. found the sternocostal head more active flat than on a decline. A 1997 study (Glass and Armstrong) is often cited for the opposite; it could not be searched (budget), so the claim states only what the three cited studies found and makes no decline recommendation.

Serratus anterior pulling the shoulder blade down: 'may' for the lowest fibres (WUSTL; Brookbush, not cited), stated flatly by LearnMuscles (not cited); one Kenhub summary said the superior part pulls the scapula down while the German Kenhub page says the superior part elevates it. No node action; the claim says 'one reference says its lowest fibres may help'.
Serratus rib count: first to eighth (TeachMeAnatomy, StatPearls), first to ninth (Elsevier), eighth or ninth (Kenhub, Radiopaedia). The claims say 'eight or nine'.
Pectoralis minor depression: 'assists' (Elsevier) against 'primarily depresses the shoulder' (StatPearls thorax muscles) and 'can forcefully depress' (Kenhub). Node action prime, noted.
Pectoralis minor innervation was given inconsistently by Kenhub pages; not used.

Poland syndrome incidence: figures differ widely between sources (StatPearls' own figure not seen), so the variation claim says 'rare' and gives no figure; side preference is not stated (copy never names a side).
